h1: What to check before offering beer home delivery in India
title: Before Offering Beer Home Delivery | Craft Beer School
desc: The licence, age checks, packaging, cold chain and delivery questions an Indian brewpub should answer before it offers beer home delivery anywhere.
teaser: Guests keep asking if you deliver. Before you say yes, check whether your licence, your packaging and your delivery partner can.
standfirst: Home delivery of beer sounds simple: fill a growler, send a rider. In India it touches state excise rules, age checks, packaging and a cold chain that has to survive the afternoon traffic. Here is what to check first.
sections: Start with the law, not the logistics

Alcohol delivery in India is decided state by state. A handful of states have allowed home delivery of liquor at various times, usually through licensed retailers and approved apps or portals, often with conditions on timing, quantity and who can deliver. Several of those permissions began as temporary measures and have since been changed or withdrawn. Most states do not allow it.

Delivery through food apps is a separate question again. A platform that delivers your biryani has no automatic right to deliver your beer. Adding beer to a food order without the right permission puts the licence at risk.

For a brewpub, the first question is narrower: does your own licence allow sale for consumption off the premises at all? Many brewpub licences allow only on-premise service. Some allow takeaway in growlers or sealed containers from the counter. Our guides to takeaway beer rules and craft beer rules by state are the right starting points. If your licence does not permit off-premise sales, delivery is not possible, however many guests ask. Check the current notification or ask a licensing consultant.
If delivery is allowed, read every condition

Where a state permits delivery, expect conditions such as:

  • Delivery only through registered platforms or the licensee's own registered staff.
  • Permits or identity cards for delivery personnel.
  • Fixed delivery hours and no delivery on dry days.
  • Limits on the quantity per order or per customer.
  • Records of each order, the buyer's details and age verification.
  • Sealed, labelled containers with brand and batch details.

Breaking any of these risks the licence that runs your whole business. That is a poor trade for a few extra growlers a week.

The legal drinking age differs between states. Delivery must never reach anyone under it. Age has to be verified at the moment of handover, not only at ordering, with valid photo identification. If the person at the door cannot show it, the beer goes back. Train every rider on this and back them when they refuse a delivery. A brewery that delivers to a minor once will not be forgiven by the excise department or the public.

Beer in an open-filled growler starts losing carbonation and picking up oxygen the moment it is filled. In the boot of a scooter on a 38 °C afternoon, it deteriorates further. Choose packaging for the journey:

  • Counter-pressure filled growlers or crowlers hold carbonation far better than open fills and keep for longer if kept cold.
  • Cans or bottles filled on a proper line are the most robust, if your licence and labelling allow them.
  • Tamper-evident seals on every container, often a legal requirement.

Our guide to growlers and crowlers covers filling methods in detail. Whatever you use, print a fill date and "keep refrigerated, best within a few days" on the label.
Keep it cold all the way

The floor detail that decides quality: beer leaves your cold room at 2 °C and should reach the customer still cold. Use insulated bags with ice packs, keep delivery radius short and do not let orders sit at the counter waiting for a rider. Test it yourself. Put a probe thermometer in a filled crowler, send it on a typical route and measure the temperature at the door. The number will tell you how far you can safely deliver.

Delivery has costs a taproom pint does not: packaging, ice packs, rider or platform fees, payment charges and breakage. Price delivered beer to cover them. Work out the contribution per order the way you would for food delivery. Set a minimum order value if needed. Compare it with the cost of keeping a tap pouring for a guest who came in.

Remember the excise and record-keeping side too. Every delivered container is a sale that has to appear correctly in your stock registers and returns. Build the delivery records into your point-of-sale system from the first day, rather than reconciling handwritten slips at the end of the month.

1. Does my licence and state policy allow off-premise sale and delivery?
  2. Who may deliver? Do they need permits?
  3. How will age be checked at the door? What happens if it fails?
  4. Does my packaging hold carbonation and seal properly?
  5. Can I keep beer cold for the longest delivery route?
  6. Do I make money on a typical order after every cost?

If any answer is unclear, wait. Delivery can be a good extra channel where it is permitted, but it sits close to the edge of your licence. That is the one asset a brewpub cannot replace.
faqs: Is beer home delivery legal in India?
It depends on the state and changes over time. Most states do not permit it. Those that have allowed it attach licences and conditions, so check the current notification.
Can a brewpub deliver growlers to customers?
Only if its licence and state policy allow off-premise sale and delivery. Many brewpub licences cover on-premise service only.
How do I keep delivered beer fresh?
Use counter-pressure filled growlers, crowlers or cans, keep them cold in insulated bags and limit the delivery radius. Test the temperature at the door on a real route.
